blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
This is our twelfth show together!
Today we fly to a zoo in Berlin, where two birthday girls share one very cold cake.
Then we tiptoe into a forest, where the trees are whispering under the ground.
Let's go!
Happy birthday, Leni and Lotti!
The twin sisters are giant pandas at Berlin Zoo.
For their second birthday, their keepers made them a cake — a cake of ice!
It had three tiers, pink and orange, coloured with beetroot and carrot juice.
On top sat little flowers carved from carrots.
No candles — pandas like presents frozen.
The sisters wasted no time.
They nibbled the carrot flowers, pawed at the ice, and chased each other around the garden.
The crowd erupted in cheers; the cameras clicked and clicked.
The children at the glass had eyes round as saucers.
At the start, the twins were tiny — born blind, almost hairless, small enough to sleep in a keeper's hand.
Leni weighed just one hundred and thirty-six grams — about as much as an apple!
Today, each sister weighs more than fifty kilos.
Their parents, Meng Meng and Jiao Qing, came from Chengdu, China — the second pair of panda twins ever born in Germany.
Every panda birthday is a party for conservation: pandas were once in great danger, and each healthy baby shows the hard work is working.
Happy birthday, Leni and Lotti — may your cake always be cold!
Now tiptoe into the forest.
Above the ground, birds sing among the leaves; below the ground, something amazing is happening.
Almost every tree is plugged into a secret network — not of wires, but of fungi: tiny threads, thinner than hair, wrapping root tips in soft nets, like little capsules of cotton.
Through it, trees trade: fungi carry water and minerals up, and trees pay with sugar from their leaves.
Nobody gets everything, but everybody gets enough.
That is a compromise — a fair deal written in sugar and water.
Scientists observed the forest for years to determine what else moves below ground.

When insects attack one tree, it sends a warning through the network — a warning relevant to every neighbour: "Make your leaves bitter — the hungry bugs are coming!" Mother trees turn up the dial and send extra sugar to their seedlings.
Is the forest really "talking"?
Not with words — but signals and supplies move from tree to tree, and the forest works like one big family.
It sounds almost like justice: the strong help the weak.
Next time you hug a tree, remember: under your feet, the forest is whispering.
Here's today's idiom: "once in a blue moon." A blue moon is a rare full moon, so this means: very rarely.
Listen: my neighbour, Mr.
Lee, washes his car once in a blue moon — maybe twice a year.
But last Sunday it rained all morning — and Mr.
Lee washed his car in the rain!
"The rain is helping me," he laughed.
And you?
What do you do once in a blue moon — once a year, not once a fortnight?
Let's think.
The panda twins shared a frozen cake; the forest shared sugar and secrets.
Two questions for you.
First: if you made a birthday cake for an animal, which animal, and what flavour?
Second: if the trees could send you one message, what would they say?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Be kind like a mother tree, and sweet like a panda's birthday.
See you tomorrow morning!
